# Diagnosing the model {#sec-diagnostics}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| cache: false
source(if (file.exists("_common.R")) "_common.R" else "chapters/_common.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: stage-banner
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
book_stage_banner("EVALUATE")
```

## Where you are

A converged fit with a sensible OFV is only a candidate. Before trusting it, check whether the model describes the data: are predictions unbiased, are residuals structureless, are the random effects well behaved and informed by the data, and are the parameters identifiable? This chapter works through these checks for the base model. It uses the fit object's tables and plain ggplot2, plus the simulation-based NPDE.

## The data

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| message: false
library(ferx)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fit
base <- ferx_example("two_cpt_oral_base")
fit <- ferx_fit(base$model, base$data, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Minimal runnable call

Most diagnostics come straight from `fit$sdtab`, which has one row per observation:

```{r}
#| label: sdtab
head(fit$sdtab)
```

`PRED` is the population prediction (all etas zero). `IPRED` is the individual prediction at the subject's estimated random effects. `CWRES` and `IWRES` are the conditional weighted and individual weighted residuals. `TAFD` and `TAD` are time after first dose and time after dose.

## Reading the result

### The fit's verdict

Before any plot, ask whether the fit can be used as it stands. `fit$converged` says that the optimizer stopped normally and, for FOCE, FOCEI, Laplace / AGQ and Gauss-Newton fits, at a stationary point: when the covariance step has an unfloored `R` matrix, ferx computes the Newton decrement at the estimate, the drop in objective a Newton step would still make, and reports `converged = FALSE` with a `W_NON_STATIONARY_OPTIMUM` warning when it is above one OFV unit ([ferx-core #2785](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2785)). `fit$status` adds what else qualifies the result: the evaluation budget, the critical warnings, the covariance step and any parameter held at a bound ([ferx-core #2799](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2799)). It is `"converged"`, `"converged_with_issues"` or `"not_converged"`, `fit$status_label` spells it as the `STATUS` line of `print()` does, and `fit$status_reasons` lists why, in a fixed order:

```{r}
#| label: status
fit[c("converged", "status", "status_label", "status_reasons")]
fit$held_at_bound
```

```{r}
#| label: check-status
#| include: false
# The sentence below: the base fit is converged with no reasons and holds no parameter.
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit$converged), identical(fit$status, "converged"), identical(fit$status_label, "CONVERGED"),
          length(fit$status_reasons) == 0, is.data.frame(fit$held_at_bound), nrow(fit$held_at_bound) == 0,
          identical(names(fit$held_at_bound), c("parameter", "kind", "index", "reason", "class")))
```

The base fit is `r fit$status_label`, with no reasons and no parameter held. A fit whose evaluation budget runs out is not. The warfarin example with `method = "focei"` and `maxiter = 2` stops early (@sec-first-fit):

```{r}
#| label: status-budget
warf <- ferx_example("warfarin")
# suppress the R warnings that report overriding the model file's method and maxiter
fit_budget <- suppressWarnings(ferx_fit(warf$model, warf$data, method = "focei",
                                        settings = list(maxiter = 2), verbose = FALSE))
fit_budget[c("converged", "status_label", "status_reasons")]
```

```{r}
#| label: check-status-budget
#| include: false
# The sentence below: the capped fit is not converged, its reasons are budget_spent and then the
# critical convergence warning.
stopifnot(!fit_budget$converged, identical(fit_budget$status, "not_converged"),
          identical(fit_budget$status_reasons, c("budget_spent", "convergence")))
# The sentence after it: a maxiter = 0 run is not_converged and carries evaluation_only.
fit_eval <- suppressWarnings(ferx_fit(base$model, base$data, settings = list(maxiter = 0), verbose = FALSE))
stopifnot(!fit_eval$converged, identical(fit_eval$status, "not_converged"),
          "evaluation_only" %in% fit_eval$status_reasons)
```

The reasons are listed for a fit that did not converge too, so they say what to fix: `budget_spent`, a larger `maxiter`, and then the critical `convergence` warning that reports it. A fit that converged but carries a reason is `"converged_with_issues"`. A run with `maxiter = 0`, which only scores the given values, is `"not_converged"` with the reason `evaluation_only`. In all, the reasons are `evaluation_only`, `budget_spent`, the category of each critical warning (including the `condition_number` warning that ferx-r raises above 1000), `covariance_failed`, and `collapsed_at_guard: <parameter>` for a variance the covariance step could not hold. `ferx_covariance()` and `ferx_load_fit()` recompute the verdict.

`fit$held_at_bound` lists every parameter the covariance step gives no standard error for, one row each: its `parameter` name, its `kind` (`"theta"`, `"omega"`, `"sigma"` or `"kappa"`), its `index` within that kind, and the `reason` ([ferx-core #2797](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2797)). The reason is `"profiled_bound"` for a profiled level held on its declared bound (@sec-mbma), or `"collapsed_at_guard"` for a variance or sigma that collapsed onto the floor ferx keeps it above, or a theta without a lower bound that sank to the internal `1e-10` floor. Such a parameter shows SE `N/A` in `print()` and `NA` in `fit$estimates`. When the covariance step is otherwise clean it holds the parameter as it holds a `FIX` one, and the other standard errors are conditional on it. The fifth column, `class`, is the class of a `[mixture]` per-class override (`omega(k)` or `sigma(k)`), whose row is labelled `<base> (class <k>)`, and `NA` for every other parameter ([ferx-core #2809](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2809)). The base fit has no such row; @sec-variability shows variances that collapse.

::: {.callout-important}
## Needs ferx-r newer than {{< var ferx_r_release >}}

`fit$status`, `fit$status_label`, `fit$status_reasons` and `fit$held_at_bound` do not exist in ferx-r {{< var ferx_r_release >}}. Its `STATUS` line shows `converged` and the categories of the critical warnings, and a parameter collapsed onto the guard gets a standard error. Its `converged` does not require a stationary point, so a fit reported converged there can be `FALSE` here, with `W_NON_STATIONARY_OPTIMUM`.
:::

### Observations against predictions

```{r}
#| label: fig-dv-pred
#| fig-cap: "Observations against population and individual predictions (log scales), with a smooth."
#| fig-width: 8
fit$sdtab |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(PRED, IPRED), names_to = "prediction", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, DV)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~prediction) +
  labs(x = "Prediction", y = "Observation")
```

Points should scatter around the identity line, and the smooth should follow it. Scatter around `PRED` also includes between-subject variability, so it is wider than around `IPRED`.

### Residuals

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: "CWRES against time and against population prediction; IWRES against individual prediction."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
library(patchwork)
res_plot <- function(x, y, xlab) {
  ggplot(fit$sdtab, aes({{ x }}, {{ y }})) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
    labs(x = xlab)
}
res_plot(TIME, CWRES, "Time (h)") + res_plot(PRED, CWRES, "PRED") + res_plot(IPRED, IWRES, "IPRED")
```

Residuals should be centred on zero with no trend over time or predictions. Most should fall within ±2, and the spread should not change with the prediction. Under a correct model CWRES are roughly standard normal:

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq-cwres
#| fig-cap: "Normal quantile plot of CWRES."
#| fig-width: 4.5
ggplot(fit$sdtab, aes(sample = CWRES)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "CWRES")
```

The fit also tests the residuals for serial correlation within subjects. `fit$dw_statistic` is the Durbin-Watson statistic of the individual residuals (`r round(fit$dw_statistic, 2)` here) and `fit$iwres_lag1_r` their lag-1 correlation (`r round(fit$iwres_lag1_r, 2)`). Both pair only consecutive observations of one subject in the same occasion (an IOV column, or the innermost level of a nested model) and, under a `correlation ... by` line, in the same residual block. The Durbin-Watson denominator counts those pairs, so independent residuals give 2 however short each subject's series is ([ferx-core #2798](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2798)). Values far from 2 and 0 respectively trigger the `dw_autocorrelation` warning this fit carries. The statistic reads in two directions, and they mean opposite things:

| `dw_statistic` | Reading | Usually points at |
|---|---|---|
| below 1.5 | Positive autocorrelation | Missing dynamics: a delay the model does not have, an absorption phase too simple, variability between occasions |
| 1.5 to 2.5 | No serial correlation worth acting on | -- |
| above 2.5 | Negative autocorrelation | Over-parameterisation, or a residual error model that does not fit the data |

::: {.callout-note}
## Changed after ferx-r {{< var ferx_r_release >}}
`fit$dw_statistic` and `fit$iwres_lag1_r` pair only consecutive residuals of one subject that share an occasion (and, under a residual `correlation` line, a residual block), and the Durbin-Watson denominator is normalised by the number of pairs, so independent residuals give 2 however short the series. ferx-r {{< var ferx_r_release >}} computes the classic form, so its values differ, and so can which fits get the `dw_autocorrelation` warning. The 1.5 and 2.5 thresholds are the same.
:::


```{r}
#| label: dw-warning
ferx_get_warnings(fit)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-dw-warning
#| include: false
# The paragraph below reads these two warnings in this order, so any other set has to fail the render.
stopifnot(identical(ferx_get_warnings(fit, as_df = TRUE)$category, c("general", "dw_autocorrelation")),
          fit$dw_statistic > 2.5, fit$iwres_lag1_r < 0)
```

The first entry is the note about the model file's `gradient = fd` that @sec-first-fit explains. The second is the residual warning: ferx suggests over-parameterisation or a misspecified residual error model as possible causes. @sec-model-selection tests alternative residual error models systematically with `ferx_ruvsearch()`.

### Individual fits

```{r}
#| label: fig-individual
#| fig-cap: "Observations (points) with individual (solid) and population (dashed) predictions for the first nine subjects."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
fit$sdtab |>
  filter(ID %in% unique(ID)[1:9]) |>
  ggplot(aes(TIME)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = DV)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = IPRED)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = PRED), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ID) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration")
```

These lines connect predictions at the observation times only. For smooth curves between samples, predict on a dense time grid with `ferx_predict()` (@sec-simulation).

### Random effects and shrinkage

`fit$ebe_etas` holds each subject's estimated random effects:

```{r}
#| label: fig-etas
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the estimated random effects."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
fit$ebe_etas |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-ID, names_to = "eta") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~eta, nrow = 1)
```

Shrinkage measures how strongly the individual estimates are pulled towards zero. High eta shrinkage means the data carry little information about that random effect for individual subjects, which makes eta-based plots (including the covariate plots below) unreliable for that parameter:

```{r}
#| label: shrinkage
data.frame(eta = fit$eta_names, shrinkage_pct = round(100 * fit$shrinkage_eta, 1))
c(eps_shrinkage_pct = round(100 * fit$shrinkage_eps, 1))
```

`fit$eta_normality` holds a Shapiro-Wilk test per eta. A flag marks p < 0.05:

```{r}
#| label: eta-normality
fit$eta_normality
```

### Random effects and covariates

`fit$eta_cov` correlates each eta with each subject-level numeric covariate in the dataset, sorted by descending |r|, and marks the pairs worth following up in its `flag` column at |r| >= 0.3. It is a quick first look for covariate relationships, and it is `NULL` when the model declares no etas, the dataset carries no usable numeric covariate, or the data file can no longer be read from `fit$data_path`:

```{r}
#| label: eta-cov
fit$eta_cov
with(fit$eta_cov, range(abs(r)[nzchar(trimws(flag))]))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-eta-cov
#| fig-cap: "Clearance random effect against body weight and creatinine clearance."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
subjects <- read.csv(base$data, na.strings = ".") |> distinct(ID, WT, CRCL)
fit$ebe_etas |>
  mutate(ID = as.integer(ID)) |>
  left_join(subjects, by = "ID") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(WT, CRCL), names_to = "covariate", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, ETA_CL)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~covariate, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL)
```

`ETA_CL` has the strongest correlations here, with `CRCL` (r = `r fit$eta_cov$r[fit$eta_cov$eta == "ETA_CL" & fit$eta_cov$covariate == "CRCL"]`) and `WT` (r = `r fit$eta_cov$r[fit$eta_cov$eta == "ETA_CL" & fit$eta_cov$covariate == "WT"]`). That motivates the covariate search in @sec-model-selection. @sec-covariates covers covariate screening tools in more detail.

### Parameter identifiability

The covariance step yields the parameter correlation matrix. Correlations near ±1 point to parameters the data cannot separate:

```{r}
#| label: fig-cor
#| fig-cap: "Correlation matrix of the parameter estimates."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
as.data.frame(as.table(fit$cor_matrix)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: identifiability
c(max_abs_correlation = fit$max_abs_correlation, condition_number = fit$condition_number)
```

The condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of this correlation matrix (`fit$eigenvalues`). ferx flags values above 1000.

### NPDE

Normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE) compare each observation with its distribution simulated under the fitted model. Unlike CWRES, they do not rely on a linearisation, and under a correct model they follow a standard normal distribution. `ferx_calc_npde()` computes them after the fit and returns the fit with `NPDE` and `NPD` columns added to `sdtab`:

```{r}
#| label: npde
fit <- ferx_calc_npde(fit, nsim = 1000, seed = 1)
summary(fit$sdtab[, c("NPDE", "NPD")])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-npde
#| fig-cap: "NPDE against time and their normal quantile plot."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
(ggplot(fit$sdtab, aes(TIME, NPDE)) +
   geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 0, 1.96), linetype = c("dotted", "dashed", "dotted")) +
   geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
   geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
   labs(x = "Time (h)")) +
  (ggplot(fit$sdtab, aes(sample = NPDE)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) + stat_qq_line() +
     labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "NPDE"))
```

`nsim` must exceed each subject's number of observations; subjects that don't get `NA` NPDE. `seed` makes the result reproducible. `model` and `data` default to the paths stored in the fit. NPDE can also be computed during the fit with the `npde_nsim` and `npde_seed` settings:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-settings-npde
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "NPDE settings."
book_settings_table(c("npde_nsim", "npde_seed"))
```

## Options that matter

| Function | Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ferx_calc_npde()` | `fit` | The fit to evaluate |
| | `nsim` | Monte Carlo replicates per subject (default 1000) |
| | `seed` | Random seed (default: the engine's) |
| | `model`, `data` | Override the model and data paths stored in the fit |
| `ferx_xpose()` | `fit` | Fit to convert |
| | `backend` | `"xpose"` (default) or `"xpose4"` |
| | `continuous`, `categorical` | Override which covariates are treated as continuous or categorical |
| | `runno` | Run number stored on the object |
| | `iterations` | Include the per-parameter optimizer trace (needs `optimizer_trace = TRUE`) |

### Using xpose

`ferx_xpose()` converts a fit into a data object for the xpose (or xpose4) diagnostics packages, which provide ready-made goodness-of-fit, parameter and covariate plots. It maps `sdtab`, the individual parameters, the random effects and the covariates to xpose's tables. xpose is not a dependency of this book, so the code is not run here:

```{r}
#| label: xpose
#| eval: false
#| eval-reason: xpose is not installed for this book (PLAN decision D2)
fit_trace <- ferx_fit(base$model, base$data, optimizer_trace = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
xpdb <- ferx_xpose(fit_trace, backend = "xpose", runno = 1, iterations = TRUE)
xpose::dv_vs_ipred(xpdb)
xpose::prm_vs_iteration(xpdb)   # parameter values over the optimizer trace
```

## Pitfalls

- **Shrinkage limits eta-based diagnostics.** When eta shrinkage is high, eta histograms and eta-covariate plots mostly show the prior, not the data.
- **Small negative shrinkage is possible.** `ETA_CL` shows `r round(100 * fit$shrinkage_eta[1], 1)`% here; this is not an error.
- **The plotted lines are not the model curve.** `sdtab` has predictions only at observation times. Use `ferx_predict()` on a dense grid for smooth individual curves.
- **`fit$eta_cov` is a screen, not a test of a covariate model.** Confirm relationships by fitting covariate models (@sec-model-selection).

### Warnings you may see here

See the ferx-core [warnings page](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/warnings.html#codes-residuals) for details.

- `dw_autocorrelation` (warning): the individual residuals are autocorrelated (Durbin-Watson out of range). Revisit the residual error or structural model.
- `eta_normality` (warning): an eta departs from normality.
- `eps_shrinkage` (warning): residual shrinkage is high or negative. Sparse data for the error model; consider simplifying it.
- `eta_shrinkage` (warning): one or more eta shrinkages exceed about 30%. The data poorly inform that variability.
- `boundary_estimate` (warning): a theta estimate sits at a bound. Relax the bound or simplify the model.
- `inflated_rse` (warning): a theta has a relative standard error above about 50%.
- `high_correlation` (warning): a pair of thetas has |correlation| ≥ 0.95.
- `condition_number` (critical): the covariance matrix is ill-conditioned. The model is likely over-parameterised.

@sec-first-fit shows a fit that carries several of these at once.

## Summary

- Plot `fit$sdtab`: observations against predictions, residuals against time and predictions, and individual fits.
- Check random effects with `fit$ebe_etas`, shrinkage and `fit$eta_normality`. Use `fit$eta_cov` for a first covariate screen.
- Check identifiability with `fit$cor_matrix` and the condition number.
- Add simulation-based NPDE with `ferx_calc_npde()`. Use `ferx_xpose()` if you work with xpose.

Next: @sec-vpc evaluates the model by simulation.
